gcTMB Methods

Usage

# S3 method for class 'gcTMB'
print(x, digits = max(3L, getOption("digits") - 3L), ...)

# S3 method for class 'gcTMB'
summary(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'summary.gcTMB'
print(x, digits = max(3L, getOption("digits") - 3L), ...)

# S3 method for class 'gcTMB'
logLik(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'gcTMB'
nobs(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'gcTMB'
df.residual(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'gcTMB'
fitted(object, random = TRUE, ...)

# S3 method for class 'gcTMB'
residuals(
  object,
  type = c("pearson", "response", "quantile", "normalized"),
  random = TRUE,
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'gcTMB'
predict(
  object,
  newdata = NULL,
  random = TRUE,
  se.fit = FALSE,
  interval = c("none", "confidence", "prediction"),
  level = 0.95,
  boot = NULL,
  nsim = 1000,
  seed = NULL,
  type = c("response", "parameters"),
  scale = c("original", "link"),
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'gcTMB'
coef(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'gcTMB'
vcov(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'gcTMB'
simulate(object, nsim = 1, seed = NULL, random = TRUE, newdata = NULL, ...)

Arguments

x, object

A gcTMB object, the result of gcTMB.

digits

Integer. Number of significant digits in the printed output

...

Not used.

random

Logical. If TRUE, the random effects are included in the predictions, fitted values and residuals (conditional residuals). TRUE corresponds to the innermost level of predict and fitted of nlme, and FALSE to level=0 (re.form=NA of lme4). For simulate, if TRUE, new random effects are drawn for each simulation, otherwise the fitted random effects are kept. For prediction intervals, random=TRUE gives the interval of a new observation in the group of each row of newdata, and random=FALSE the interval of a new observation in a new group, including the variance of the random effects. Rows of newdata with a level that is not in the fitted data are treated as new groups for that random effect term.

type

Character string. For residuals, the type of residuals: "pearson" (default), the response residuals divided by the standard deviation of the fitted distribution and multiplied by the square root of the weights; "response", the observed minus the fitted values, as proportions for a binomial response; or "quantile", randomised quantile residuals (Dunn and Smyth, 1996), which are standard normal under the model. The types "response", "pearson" and "normalized" are those of residuals of nlme. "normalized" (gaussian and lognormal) are the standardised residuals decorrelated by the autocorrelation of the fit (see corStruct): each standardised residual minus rho^dt times the previous one of its group, divided by sqrt(1 - rho^(2 dt)), independent standard normal under the model, as in nlme; without autocorrelation they are the pearson residuals, and so for the other families. For the gaussian family, the quantile residuals are multiplied by the square root of the weights, as precision weights with standard deviation sigma/sqrt(w); for the other families they do not use the weights, as a weighted log-likelihood is not the density of a distribution of the observation. The quantile residuals are random for the count families; use set.seed for reproducible values. For the lognormal family, the pearson and quantile residuals are the standardised residuals of log(y), (log(y) - log(f))/sigma, multiplied by the square root of the weights. For predict, the type of prediction: "response" (default), the mean response at the times of newdata, or "parameters", the parameters b1-b3 of the curve of each row of newdata (with its covariates in fform and, with random=TRUE, the random effects of its groups); newdata then needs no time. The standard errors of the parameters are those of the estimates, by the delta method, and their confidence intervals are computed on the scale of the link and back-transformed; with random=TRUE, they include the uncertainty of the predicted random effects of the fitted groups. Prediction intervals of the parameters add the variance of the random effects of the terms without a fitted level, the parameters of a new group, and are not available with boot.

newdata

Data frame or NULL. The data for the predictions, with the time and the covariates of the model. If NULL, the original data is used. For simulate, the times, covariates and grouping variables of the observations to simulate, e.g. new times or new individuals; each level of a grouping variable is one curve, with random effects shared by its rows. With random=TRUE all levels get new random effects; with random=FALSE the levels in the fitted data keep their fitted random effects and the other levels get new ones. For binomial responses the number of trials is taken from the response in newdata (one for a binary response).

se.fit

Logical. If TRUE, predict returns the standard errors of the predicted means, by the delta method; with random=TRUE they include the uncertainty of the predicted random effects.

interval

Character string. The type of interval of predict: "none", "confidence" for confidence intervals of the mean, computed on the log scale for poisson and lognormal and on the logit scale for binomial and beta responses, or "prediction" for prediction intervals of a new observation with weight 1. Gaussian and lognormal models without random effects use t quantiles with n - p degrees of freedom and the unbiased residual variance, see gcTMB. For the gaussian and lognormal (on the log scale) families without boot, the prediction intervals use the normal (or t) distribution, and the variance of the random effects of new groups is added by the delta method. Otherwise they are quantiles of new observations simulated at nsim draws from the normal approximation of the fixed and random effects, with the variance parameters kept at their estimates, or at the bootstrap fits (see boot); with new random effects for new groups; for a binomial response as proportions, with the number of trials from the response in newdata (one for a binary response).

level

Numeric between 0 and 1. Confidence level of the intervals of predict

boot

A bootstrap.gcTMB object or NULL. A bootstrap sample of the model from bootstrap. predict then gives the standard deviation of the bootstrap predictions as se.fit, percentile confidence intervals, and prediction intervals simulated at the bootstrap fits, including their variance parameters. The bootstrap responses have new random effects, so for random=TRUE the random effects of the fitted groups are drawn, for each bootstrap fit, from the Laplace approximation of their conditional distribution given the original data at the parameters of that fit.

nsim

Integer. Number of response vectors to simulate; for predict, the number of parameter draws for simulated prediction intervals

seed

Integer or NULL. An optional seed for the random number generator

scale

Character string. For type="parameters", the scale of the parameters: "original" (default) or "link", the scale of the coefficients, see the argument link of gcTMB.

Value

Estimated model coefficients, variance-covariance matrix, or predictions. predict returns a vector of predicted means, or, with se.fit=TRUE or an interval, a data frame with the predicted means (fit), their standard errors (se.fit), and the limits of the intervals (lwr, upr). With type="parameters", it returns a matrix of the parameters used by the model, a row for each row of newdata, or, with se.fit=TRUE or an interval, a data frame with the row of newdata (row), the parameter, and fit, se.fit, lwr and upr. coef and vcov include the variance parameters (unlike coef of nlme and lme4, coef does not return the coefficients of each group; see predict(type="parameters")): for each random effect term the log standard deviations (log_sd:b1|group, or log_sd:b1:x|group for a random slope of b1 in x) and, for correlated random effects, the parameters of the correlation matrix (corr_par:b2,b1|group, unconstrained elements of the lower triangle of its Cholesky factor, by row); and the log residual standard deviation (log_sigma, gaussian; of log(y) for lognormal), log precision (log_phi, beta), log size (log_theta, nbinom2), log dispersion (log_phi, nbinom1) or log precision (log_phi, betabinomial); and for an estimated autocorrelation the parameter cor_par:AR1 or cor_par:CAR1 on the unconstrained scale of nlme (coef of an nlme corStruct), see corStruct. summary returns a summary.gcTMB object with the coefficient table (Estimate, Std. Error), the variance components, log-likelihood, AIC and BIC, sample sizes, a Pearson dispersion statistic for poisson and binomial models, and convergence information. logLik returns the log-likelihood at the estimates, with the number of free coefficients and variance parameters as degrees of freedom; it is the maximum likelihood, comparable with nlme fits with method="ML", not with the REML fits of nlme::lme and nlme::gls. df.residual returns the residual degrees of freedom n - p of gaussian and lognormal models without random effects (small-sample inference, see gcTMB), and NULL otherwise; as the df argument of multcomp::glht for the times of timeto, it gives multivariate t instead of normal quantiles. simulate returns a data frame with nsim columns of simulated responses at the estimated parameters (or those set by update.gcTMB), a row for each observation of the fit or row of newdata; for a binomial response given as cbind(successes, failures), the number of successes. Its attribute ranef has the random effects of each simulation, a list named like the columns with an element in the format of ranef (for random=FALSE, the fitted random effects of the fitted levels), and its attribute mean the true means of the simulated responses, a data frame like the simulations: the curve f(t) of each observation with its random effects (the median for lognormal; for binomial and beta-binomial responses the proportion).

Examples

fit <- gcTMB(height ~ DAS, rform=b1 + b2 ~ 1 | plant_ID, data=FabaHeights25)
summary(fit)
#> Call:
#> gcTMB(form = height ~ DAS, rform = b1 + b2 ~ 1 | plant_ID, data = FabaHeights25)
#> 
#> Model:  logistic, truncated at b4 = 0
#> Family: gaussian, identity link for all parameters
#> 
#> Number of observations: 200, groups: plant_ID 25
#> Log-likelihood: -513.7 (df = 7), AIC: 1041, BIC: 1064
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>                Estimate Std. Error
#> b1:(Intercept)   121.09      2.257
#> b2:(Intercept)    30.87      0.542
#> b3:(Intercept)    12.84      0.250
#> 
#> Random effects:
#>  Groups   Name Std.Dev. Corr 
#>  plant_ID b1   10.237        
#>           b2    2.561   -0.12
#> 
#> Residual standard deviation: 2.074
#> 
#> Optimiser: relative convergence (4), maximum absolute gradient 8.4e-05
coef(fit)
#>          b1:(Intercept)          b2:(Intercept)          b3:(Intercept) 
#>             121.0884446              30.8662604              12.8414641 
#>      log_sd:b1|plant_ID      log_sd:b2|plant_ID corr_par:b2,b1|plant_ID 
#>               2.3259984               0.9403950              -0.1214161 
#>               log_sigma 
#>               0.7294995 
logLik(fit)
#> 'log Lik.' -513.6748 (df=7)
# the population curve with confidence and prediction intervals
nd <- data.frame(DAS=c(20, 40, 60))
predict(fit, newdata=nd, random=FALSE, interval="confidence")
#>         fit   se.fit       lwr       upr
#> 1  28.69590 1.021166  26.69445  30.69735
#> 2  77.60741 1.772894  74.13260  81.08221
#> 3 108.71077 1.958312 104.87254 112.54899
predict(fit, newdata=nd, random=FALSE, interval="prediction")
#>         fit   se.fit      lwr       upr
#> 1  28.69590 1.021166 18.03090  39.36089
#> 2  77.60741 1.772894 59.58726  95.62755
#> 3 108.71077 1.958312 88.99044 128.43109
# the curve of plant 6, and its parameters
predict(fit, newdata=data.frame(DAS=c(20, 40, 60), plant_ID=6))
#> [1]  29.42109  81.76640 116.58430
predict(fit, newdata=data.frame(plant_ID=6), type="parameters")
#>           b1       b2       b3
#> [1,] 130.789 31.81211 12.84146
head(residuals(fit, type="quantile"))
#> [1]  0.7935475  1.1835400  0.7464733  0.3406020 -0.7506480  0.8659088
dim(simulate(fit, nsim=5, seed=1))
#> [1] 200   5
# three new plants at new times
nd <- expand.grid(DAS=seq(10, 80, 10), plant_ID=c("new1", "new2", "new3"))
sims <- simulate(fit, nsim=2, seed=1, newdata=nd)
head(sims)
#>       sim_1     sim_2
#> 1  15.84609  8.366161
#> 2  39.14342 24.477550
#> 3  66.27427 47.961726
#> 4  89.36434 69.243148
#> 5 110.53706 84.621353
#> 6 118.26703 95.285112
# the simulated random effects of the first simulation, and the true curves
attr(sims, "ranef")$sim_1
#> $plant_ID
#>             b1         b2
#> new1  6.282544 -4.2577268
#> new2 -1.906770 -0.7764702
#> new3  8.620931  1.8089401
#> 
head(attr(sims, "mean"))
#>       sim_1     sim_2
#> 1  14.83514  9.183935
#> 2  37.61210 24.600568
#> 3  65.08007 45.680227
#> 4  89.99773 67.660289
#> 5 107.40156 84.962581
#> 6 117.45848 95.810595
